title: Light for the Clock and the Pupil

scenes.visual: Title: Light for the Clock and the Pupil.

scenes.tts: Take a mouse with no working rods or cones. It still responds to light. Its body clock still shifts with day and night, and its pupils still narrow in bright light. A small set of retinal ganglion cells is doing this. They carry their own light pigment, called melanopsin. In mice, they are the retina's main route for setting the body clock, and they drive the pupil reflex. They report how bright the world is, not what is in it.
scenes.visual: Mouse retina chain: rod and cone, bipolar, ganglion cell, brain. Rod and cone crossed out. A clock and a pupil still respond to light. The ganglion cell lights up with melanopsin; label: non-image-forming.

scenes.tts: These cells are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ip R G Cs. An ip R G C makes its own light response with melanopsin. It also relays signals that rods and cones send through bipolar cells. So it has two jobs. Hold on to that. It explains everything that follows.
scenes.visual: One large ipRGC. Green route: own melanopsin response. Blue route: rod and cone signals via a bipolar cell.
scenes.narration: These cells are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ipRGCs. An ipRGC makes its own light response with melanopsin. It also relays signals that rods and cones send through bipolar cells. So it has two jobs. Hold on to that. It explains everything that follows.
scenes.caption: These cells are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ipRGCs. An ipRGC makes its own light response with melanopsin. It also relays signals that rods and cones send through bipolar cells. So it has two jobs. Hold on to that. It explains everything that follows.

scenes.tts: Where do these signals go? ip R G C axons reach the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master clock. Light arriving there keeps the clock in step with day and night. That is called photoentrainment. Other ip R G C axons reach the olivary pretectal nucleus, which narrows the pupil. The two routes can be pulled apart. Remove one genetically marked set of these cells, and the pupil reflex fails badly. The clock still entrains.
scenes.visual: ipRGC axons split: one to an SCN box with a clock icon, one to an olivary pretectal nucleus box with a pupil icon. Then the pupil branch greys out while the clock branch stays lit.

scenes.tts: How do we know the cells matter? Compare two experiments. Take away only melanopsin. The mice still entrain, but their clock shifts less after a brief light pulse, and in steady bright light their pupils slowly widen again. Now take away the cells themselves, and leave rods and cones intact. The clock and pupil deficits are larger, much like mice that lack melanopsin, rods and cones together.
scenes.visual: Panel one: ipRGC with melanopsin crossed out, relay route intact; clock shifts less, pupil narrows then slowly widens. Panel two: ipRGC removed, both routes crossed; clock and pupil icons both greyed.

scenes.tts: So rods and cones send their clock and pupil signals through these cells, and melanopsin holds the pupil steady in bright light. Taking out the pigment removes one job. Taking out the cells removes both. That is why removing the cells and removing the pigment answer different questions. When you can, remove them in adult animals, because loss during development can rewire targets.
scenes.visual: Summary diagram: rods and cones and melanopsin both feed the ipRGC, which feeds clock and pupil. Two chips: 'remove pigment = one job', 'remove cells = both'. Adult timed chip.

scenes.tts: In mice, these cells also affect mood and learning, apparently by two separate routes. A smaller story asks about seeing patterns. Mice lacking rod and cone signalling could tell a grating from plain grey, and mice lacking melanopsin showed contrast deficits. That is very coarse vision, not normal acuity. The main job of these cells is still the clock and the pupil.
scenes.visual: Two small side branches from the ipRGC: mood and learning (mouse icon). A faint grating-versus-grey panel labelled 'coarse only'. Final frame returns to the clock and pupil icons.
